item.title: A reply to Austin Chen on his “keen debt” to FTX when hiring Caroline Ellison at Manifund
item.description:
Published on September 30, 2026 8:55 PM GMT

New account here, created by an irate outsider to EA.

I started typing this as a response to a comment by Austin, in the discussion of his recent shocking announcement that his organization Manifund has hired Caroline Ellison. My reply to him ballooned to a size that merits its own post.

Please bear with me as I attempt to somewhat match this forum’s style. I will be consolidating some of the points that I and others have made less charitably on X and other sites.

--

General context:

Caroline Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda Research, was one of the convicted perpetrators of the FTX cryptocurrency fraud, along with her boss Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) and two complicit software engineers. Together, these four EAs stole billions of dollars from FTX’s customers.

Austin Chen co-founded the Manifold prediction market, which received money from FTX, and he subsequently moved on to create a non-profit called Manifund (formally, Manifold For Charity), where Caroline Ellison now works for him.

--

Austin, I'm going to respond to this bluntly, even though I believe you meant well. This action creates an unacceptable flow of funds and benefits, starting with the FTX victims and ending with one of the people who defrauded them.

Nothing that follows is directed personally against Caroline Ellison, whom I happen to have known many years ago and don't resent. She did her time. Her contrition seemed to be on the genuine side. She is smarter and more self-assertive than she was made out to be, both by the press and by her own defense strategy. It’s my opinion that EAs – who sit somewhere on the long list of people she harmed with her crimes – may forgive her if they so choose. No pressure. The quality of mercy is not strained.

More generally, I believe that FTX was not primarily about the criminals themselves. EA's main failure at FTX is not that they let four bad people into their good people club. EA’s main failure is that the philosophy, as it turns out, can accidentally inspire big crimes, and EAs needed to reflect on that. Some have, rarely enough. But that's a separate discussion.

Caroline is not an ogre, and Austin, if you can convince Manifund’s stakeholders of your plan for governance in this highly irregular situation, then as far as I care, you can go ahead and employ her...

Except:

First, you need to give back the $500,000 grant. All of it.

This repayment will correspond to the July/August 2022 grant of $500k from FTX to Manifold, where you were a co-founder. Maybe the claim is more like $508k, as stated in the court filings, apparently to cover some additional prize payouts in October, shortly before FTX's collapse that November. Pay the whole bill. 

There's also the separate matter of the "seed funding", apparently around $1 million, that Manifold received earlier in 2022 from FTX/Alameda’s venture arm. I can’t tell whether this stake is still held by the FTX bankruptcy estate, or whether the estate is treating it as another donation and lumping it in together with the $500k claim. Clearly you and your Manifold friends need to resolve this equity obligation too; however, it sounds like the sort of gnarly thing that will take time, given the multiple parties involved. I expect it will happen according to an acceptable process, so I am leaving it out of this post.[1]

But as for the $500k grant, you should find a way to pay it back independently, out of your own end. The need to repay it is obvious to me as an outsider, but I'm going to lay out the case to you here with the full verbosity for which this forum and its elder counterpart are famous.

A quick note about alternative facts

As an aside: I am also concerned by your past statements defending SBF’s actions, both in your contrarian post three days after the bankruptcy when any sensible observer could already see that fraud had been committed, and in the years since.

I am tempted to ask you whether have ever accepted the plain reality of these infamous events: that FTX was a real crime, not just a mistake; that the crimes started within months of the exchange’s founding in 2019, and escalated thereafter; that FTX was not a bank and so the subsequent performance of any investments has no bearing on the criminality; that the depositors have not been fully repaid in a true economic sense; that SBF took risks that were not his to take; that Michael Lewis got taken for a ride; that CZ’s role was incidental to Sam’s self-inflicted downfall; and that it is only through quirks of the legal process that EA and rationalist orgs have been able to keep so much of the money.[2]

But it doesn't seem productive to insist that you affirm these facts when you may or may not believe them, and moreover, you say you’ve been legally advised not to discuss your opinions in detail. So I will give you the benefit of the doubt and just assume that by now, your professed admiration of FTX is mainly directed at certain innovations by the giving arm, and I will return my focus to the more tangible request here, which is that you repay the money.

Actions speak louder than words, after all.

The chain of obligation

Let’s start by reviewing the history of how all these assets got mixed together. I am not speaking in a technical legal sense of “commingled” or whatever, but rather in a functional, moral sense, which is probably more stringent.

  1. In July/August of 2019, Nishad Singh wrote the backdoor loophole code. Thereafter, all money leaving either FTX or Alameda was functionally indistinguishable from FTX user funds. (There was theoretically a limit to the loophole, but SBF and Gary Wang could and did increase that limit at will, so the borrowing from FTX users was functionally unlimited.)[3]
  2. By June 2022 at the latest, it was clear to SBF and Caroline Ellison that there was an $8 billion hole in their balance sheet.
  3. In July/August of 2022, FTX’s philanthropy team paid $500k of these FTX user funds to Manifold, the prediction exchange where Austin Chen was a co-founder. As phrased, this grant was largely intended for regifting, but from another perspective, it was a perk and an inducement for the power-users on your growing exchange platform. It was also free publicity. Under the circumstances, we must take the least favorable perspective.
  4. Anything that Manifold paid Austin in salary or equity, up to $500k, was functionally FTX user funds.
  5. Anything that Austin took (or will take) with him to Manifund was FTX user funds, up to $500k. This may include the opportunity cost of switching from a for-profit role to a new non-profit.
  6. Anything that Manifund is paying Caroline – whether it’s salary, or in-kind as work experience and rehabilitation, up to $500k – is FTX user funds.

Again, we are not in a civil court here, and I’m not opining on the ongoing litigation. Rather, we are in this unprecedented instance where a fraudster is being welcomed back into her old clique with warm expressions of gratitude. We need to look at each step in this chain through the least charitable lens. We should count the intangibles against you. In the broadest possible way, we must acknowledge here that money is fungible.

Note that in Step (3) above, Caroline does not seem to have personally directed the grant money to Manifold. Rather, it was Will MacAskill and Leopold Aschenbrenner, working at the FTX Future Fund, who signed off on it. If we asked them, I doubt that they would say that their intent was to provide for a future soft landing after prison for FTX/Alameda executives in a scenario where SBF turned out to be running a big fraud. They didn’t know!

But we’re not talking about an explicit deal; we’re talking about a general spirit of reciprocation. When the fraudsters were spreading all this money around the EA ecosystem, even turning up the firehose in some cases as they realized the size of the Alameda balance sheet hole, their motives were surely mixed. I have high confidence that SBF and his comrades really believed in the EA causes they sponsored, but it’s reasonable to speculate that they were also hoping to cultivate a store of goodwill among EAs, which could be called upon in the increasingly likely event that their scheme fell apart. Regardless of their exact mix of motives, it would be highly improper to reward this behavior by the four fraudsters.

You, Austin – and by extension EA, for all an outsider might care – need to be totally, thoroughly beyond conflict of interest, before you even try to rehabilitate a friend who is a party to an $11 billion fraud. You – and by extension, EA – need to be totally, thoroughly beyond the hint of an implicit quid pro quo.

One could probably go even further. As described in your announcement, you received other benefits as well – a conference, a retreat, opportunities, and so forth. One could assess the cash value of your Bahamas trip. One could also investigate whether any other donor money that will flow through Caroline’s hands at Manifund is partially downstream of other FTX grants, as is inevitable when handling EA money.[4] But I think that’s all probably de minimis, in the grand scheme. If you err on the side of overpaying by returning the full $500k, I believe it would easily cover these other conflicts, too.

Your good intentions

As I said at the outset, it’s clear to me that you truly believe you’re doing the right thing by giving Caroline a second chance. I have met you a few times, and you came across as kind and humble. You have done things that I thought were neat. [5] What I know of your work has often involved you standing by your stated principles. And in making this unconventional hiring decision, I think you’re trying to live by principles such as gratitude, loyalty, reciprocity, fairness, and forgiveness. This is respectable, except that here, the principles are grossly misapplied.

If someone does you a favor, it is natural to want to pay it back. If someone does you a favor using stolen money, then it is no longer correct to pay her back, at least not until you’ve done your best to make the primary victims whole. It is certainly not okay to pay her back with the money that she stole.

As you cling to the bulk of this $500k that was given to Manifold, maybe your stubborn attitude comes partly from a sense of fairness. Maybe it’s not “fair” that you were on the verge of getting to some settlement that would let you and your former colleagues at Manifold off the hook for most of the $500k. If the judicial process is definitionally “fair”, then paying anything extra must feel unjust.

Maybe it doesn’t seem “fair” that the bankruptcy team has tried for years to pierce through the dual nature of the FTX regranting landscape.  On the one hand, it was a creative way to distribute funds through a network of trusted deciders – a technique which Manifund, incidentally, has copied and iterated upon, with what I’m told are promising results. On the other hand, it had the effect of splitting up the stolen money among thousands of little entities, behind several layers of proxy, making repayment arduous, and letting an entity like Manifold shrug and say they don’t have the money anymore. It might not seem “fair” to you that the cleanest recourse for the creditors is to just sue the first recipient for the full sum. But sadly, that’s a peril of doing regranting for a reckless and duplicitous guy like Sam.

From the outside, to be frank, it’s quite infuriating that in the good times, whenever all of the EAs and rationalists are trying to save the world, it’s one big team with everyone largely supporting each other, but then as soon as someone does a crime or owes money, suddenly none of these orgs have ever heard of one another.

Anyhow, Austin, let me bring up your explanatory comment that I began typing this post in response to. In it, you lay out the stats of Lightcone Infrastructure’s settlement with the FTX bankruptcy team. You offer up their stats “[f]or reference”, as if it’s some sort of relevant benchmark. By your numbers, it seems that Lightcone returned around 40% of what they got from FTX, and kept the rest.[6]

Maybe it doesn't feel “fair” to you that Lightcone got away with over half of their haul, and you're being asked to pay your whole bill. But Lightcone is not employing Caroline. Lightcone's share of the loot is not flowing brazenly into the hands of one of the perpetrators. Lightcone did not write a forum post that basically says "QUID PRO QUO" in giant bold letters for all the world to see, rubbing it in the face of any FTX depositor who reads it. I suppose we should applaud your honesty about your motives, but if this flow of funds weren’t already damning on its own, your shameless rationale would seal the deal.[7]

The point is, what’s fair for Lightcone and other orgs is not what’s fair for you. The bar is higher for you now, if you want to pay Caroline even one dollar.

Lastly, in hiring Caroline, I do think that you’re sincerely trying to demonstrate some virtue like Christian mercy and forgiveness. I can honestly see the case for that, in isolation.

But in the complexity of our lives, context matters. Under the current circumstances, it is not your place to dispense mercy. You are sitting, in your own words, upon a “keen debt” to FTX. While I imagine the turmoil of the FTX bankruptcy has been rough on you, you are not a primary victim of the fraud. You do not have the standing to forgive her in this manner.

Buy yourself that standing, Austin, if you like. If you truly believe in this grand gesture of yours, then pay up, more than may be legalistically required of you.

Those are the main principles that I think are being misapplied.[8] Now, let’s turn now to the future. You have three options at this juncture, as I see it.

Option 1: Dismiss Caroline

Bow to the pressure and amicably part ways with her.

As I understand your motives, I doubt this is what you wish to do. There are plenty of people in these comment sections who want to see her head on a figurative pike, and maybe yours as well. Their reasons are quite robust. But I sense that you've dug your heels deeply into what you see as a principled stand.

Again, I can respect your intransigence. It would be in character for you! Consider the controversies around your platforming choices at the Manifest conference, which people have dredged up in their reactions to this hiring announcement. As much as I disagree with those radioactive personalities whom you allowed to attend and speak, I can appreciate the principle at play: Free exchange of ideas has always been a rationalist value.

Of course, the attempt to “cancel” your conference over questions of speech was quite a different beast from people’s desire to dissociate from you now based on your intolerable actions. And of course, your attempt to divert the current discussion into that well-trod territory of Manifest speakers was squirrelly and obvious. You’re better than that. Repairing trust will take more than just thanking people for their criticism and then deflecting.

But anyway, I think there is a narrow parallel here. With Caroline as with the Manifest speakers, you seem to be determined to take an unpopular course of action no matter if it’s costly.

So why not pay the cost?

Option 2: Pay back the $500k to the FTX creditors

Work with Manifold to get this grant money back to the FTX bankruptcy entity – not as a drawn-out settlement, but as a unilateral concession. It should come from yourself, as the one who is passing on this improper flow to Caroline, rather than from anyone else on the Manifold cap table. I hope that the various parties can find a way to minimize the disruption to your other legal wranglings as you do this.[9]

As someone who has run an exchange and understands markets, you surely know that the creditors have not been fully repaid in a true economic sense, because FTX itself caused the artificially low dollar value marks at the moment that Sam admitted defeat. I’d be happy to elaborate if it’s unclear.

Perhaps your attempt to keep some of the Manifold grant money feels like yet another principled stand to you, similar to hiring Caroline. I could probably steelman each of these two defiant stances independently. But when the two actions are put together in the full context of your entanglement with FTX, your stance against full repayment has far less merit.

Incidentally, I would argue that repaying the depositors is a worthy act on its own merits. Indeed, if repaying the victims of EA – beyond what is exacted legally – is never an EA cause area, why would any normal person trust EAs to align a lawnmower, much less an AGI?

Perhaps restitution doesn’t strike an EA as the most “effective” cause. Perhaps you know how to spend this money better than the FTX creditors. But we should be skeptical of any belief that even faintly echoes SBF’s apparent attitude, whereby it is justified for EAs to take and invest other people’s money because EAs will use it in smarter and more altruistic ways.

Please bear with me as I attempt to somewhat match this forum’s style. I will be consolidating some of the points that I and others have made less charitably on X and other sites.

--

Published on October 1, 2026 10:52 AM GMT

Summary

Over the course of a year, the Fieldshaper program develops you into a field-leading grantmaker. You’ll steward $1,000,000 in grant capital, receive a $125,000 annual stipend, and deploy that capital within a sub-field of one of three key areas (farmed animals, global health, or philanthropic infrastructure); building the track record to become a grantmaker who can shape a field.

Currently, there is no clear pathway for someone to get started into the field, and we see this long-term career impact as the primary driver of this program’s impact.

Traits

  • Rigor and intellectual honesty under ambiguity; decision-making grounded in evidence.
  • Clear decision-making grounded in evidence and logic.
  • Comfort with the responsibility of directing large amounts of capital.
  • Ability to do high-quality self-directed work and gain knowledge quickly in a field.
  • No prior grantmaking experience required (we are equally excited about applicants who have none).

Mid-career Professionals

Profile: Mid-career, currently in an adjacent sector (consulting, entrepreneurship, tech, policy) and looking for a structured route into philanthropy. Concrete example: An ex-consultant who did three years of consulting and then founded her own firm. She is exceptional at the work and disappointed by its lack of impact. She has been filling evenings and weekends with volunteering and reading about social issues online. She has not picked a cause area and grantmaking feels like the best nonprofit role that would check boxes she has in terms of risk, intellectual challenge and impact at the same time. However, the path to get there is completely unclear.

Profile: People who have founded, run, or held senior operating roles at high-impact, evidence-based nonprofits and now want to move to the funding side. Applications are open now, and close October 30th. We aim to have acceptance offers out to candidates by mid-December, with the program starting in February.

  3. Two interviews
  4. Two test tasks
  5. References

item.title: GiveWell fundraising up 49% in 2025, driven overwhelmingly by 39 donors giving $1M+
item.description:
Published on October 2, 2026 9:19 PM GMT

Previously: GiveWell raised less than its 10th percentile forecast in 2023 · GiveWell fundraising up 17% in 2024

GiveWell has published its 2025 metrics, together with a metrics report and a public spreadsheet. As in previous years, I focus on how much was raised and who gave it. This year I also look at how concentrated GiveWell's donor base is.

Truth be told I kinda phoned it in on this one, the full Claude version with better charts is here

Summary

  • Returning donors gave $443.6M (up 77%). New donors gave $37.1M (up 112%), which is still below their 2020–2022 levels.
  • 39 donors giving $1M or more contributed $359.7M. That is 75% of identified donations through GiveWell and 90% of the year's increase. Every smaller size band also grew, by 13–27%.
  • The donor base is far more concentrated than an 80/20 rule. The top 20% of donors gave about 97% of the money, and about 0.26% of donors (roughly 90) gave 80%. Asking the question again within the top group (the top 20% of the top 20%, and so on) gives 94%, 93% and 92%, rather than 80% each time.

Returning donors drove the increase

Returning donors gave $443.6M, up 77% on 2024. That is 72% of all funds raised and 86% of the money from donors other than Coefficient Giving, both the highest shares in the series. The average returning donor gave about $20,800, against $12,300 in 2024.

New donors gave $37.1M, up 112%. This reverses three years of decline ($41.2M in 2022, $20.5M in 2023, $17.5M in 2024), but it remains below 2020–2022 levels. Anonymous giving fell 7% to $35.6M.

The number of donors rose for the first time since 2021. There were 13,796 new donors (up 34%) and 21,315 returning donors, a record. Together that makes 35,111 identified donors, up 14%, but still below the 2021 peak of about 41,900.

The increase was driven overwhelmingly by $1M+ donations

GiveWell reports donations that pass through its own accounts by donor size, with each donor placed in a band by their total gifts in the year. On this measure, identified donations rose by $230.4M, from $246.7M to $477.1M.

  • $1M+ donors: 39 (up from 26) gave $359.7M, up 138%. That accounts for $208.4M, or 90%, of the increase. The average gift in this band rose from $5.8M to $9.2M, so the growth came both from more very large donors and from larger gifts.
  • Every smaller band also grew: $100K–$1M by 27%, $10K–$100K by 23%, $1K–$10K by 19%, $100–$1K by 14% and under $100 by 13%. Giving below $1M rose 23% in total, against 10% in 2024, so growth was broader than last year even though the top band dominated it.
  • The $1M+ share of identified donations through GiveWell rose from 43% in 2020 to 61% in 2024 and 75% in 2025.

 

Is GiveWell's funding 80/20? No: it is far more concentrated

An 80/20 rule means the top 20% of donors give 80% of the money. If donations followed a Pareto distribution with that property, the pattern would repeat at every scale. The top 20% of the top 20% (4% of donors) would give 80% of that group's money, which is 64% of the total. The next level down (0.8% of donors) would give 51% of the total, and so on.

The size bands give exact figures only at their boundaries ($100, $1K, $10K, $100K and $1M). I interpolated between them (see the methodology section) and report ranges where the data leave room for doubt. For 2025:

  • The top 20% of donors (about 7,000) gave about 97% of the money (range 96.0–97.7%).
  • About 0.26% of donors, roughly 90 people or entities, gave 80% of the money (range 61–136 donors). In 2020–2024 the equivalent figure was 1.5–3.0% of donors.
  • The 39 donors giving $1M+, 0.11% of donors, gave 75%. This figure is exact.

Pareto within Pareto

Next, I asked the question again within each successive top group. At each level, what share of the group's money did the top 20% of that group give?

At every level the data can resolve, 2025 is well above 80%, and even the conservative end of each range is about 90%. Concentration has also risen over time. In 2020 the fourth level was almost exactly 80/20 (80.9%); in 2025 it was 91.5%. Beyond level 4 (about 11 donors, then about 2) the published bands cannot distinguish between very different distributions, so I do not report those levels.

Among the very largest donors, the distribution is close to a textbook 80/20. If the $1M+ band follows a Pareto tail, its average gift of $9.2M implies a tail index of α ≈ 1.12. An exact 80/20 rule corresponds to α ≈ 1.16. The largest donors are therefore slightly more concentrated than 80/20 among themselves. In earlier years α was about 1.19–1.28, slightly less concentrated than 80/20. The overall figure is so extreme because more than 30,000 donors give under $10K each, and together they account for under 7% of the money.

The figures above exclude Coefficient Giving. If its $100M is counted as a single additional donor, 80% of the combined money came from about 0.12% of donors (about 42). The nested shares rise to 98%, 95%, 94% and 93%.

Methodology and caveats

  • Data. The concentration analysis uses the spreadsheet's "Donations through GiveWell by Donor Size" tables, which give amounts and donor counts for identified donors. In 2025 these cover 35,098 donors and $477.1M. They exclude anonymous gifts ($18.9M through GiveWell), direct-to-charity gifts (for which no donor counts are published) and Coefficient Giving's $100M, which went directly to charities.
  • Interpolation. Within each band I assumed a truncated power-law distribution matched to the band's average gift. For the $1M+ band I assumed a Pareto tail with α = mean ÷ (mean − $1M). The ranges are the lowest and highest values consistent with the band counts and totals alone, with no distributional assumption.
  • What counts as a donor. The report does not say how foundations, donor-advised funds or effective-giving organisations are counted. If some $1M+ "donors" are intermediaries passing on many individuals' gifts, concentration among individuals is overstated. I would welcome clarification from GiveWell.
  • 2024 comparability. In the spreadsheet, 2024 donations through GiveWell ($255.8M) are about $8.2M more than non-Open Philanthropy giving minus direct-to-charity gifts. The 2024 size bands therefore appear to include about $8.2M of Open Philanthropy money, most likely in the $1M+ band. The 2025 bands include $39,625 from Coefficient Giving.
  • Metrics year. GiveWell's metrics year runs from 1 February to 31 January, so "2025" means 1 February 2025 to 31 January 2026.

Sources

  • GiveWell, GiveWell's 2025 Metrics and Impact (31 August 2026)
  • GiveWell, Metrics Report 2025 and Tables for the 2025 Metrics Report
  • GiveWell, Metrics Report 2024
  • GiveWell, How much funding does GiveWell expect to raise through 2025? (10 April 2023)
  • GiveWell, Coefficient Giving Commits $175 Million to GiveWell Opportunities (18 December 2025)
  • GiveWell, Scaling Our Impact, with Support from a $1 Billion Commitment (23 July 2026)

item.title: What I learned from going on 230 dates with EAs
item.description:
Published on October 5, 2026 2:30 PM GMT

A conflict of interest to flag: I'm the founder of Settled, a relationship and matchmaking company with free and paid tiers.  That may create bias in what I notice and what I recommend, so weigh these recommendations accordingly.  I’d love for some of you to sign up to Settled, but my aim here is to share something useful whether or not you ever do.
 

What this post is and isn’t 

  • We’re writing this because we hope it provide helpful insights - people have also asked, so here it is!
  • This post is based on:
    • Hundreds of hours of interviews and coaching  with 350+ singles
    • Data from Settled: nearly 2K completed questionnaires & hundreds of feedback forms from dates we set up
    • An ongoing literature review (with help from Claude) - 70+ papers reviewed

item.description:
Published on October 5, 2026 3:01 PM GMT

Cross-posted from my substack. 

Today, I’m launching the Wildlife Technology Fund at Renaissance Philanthropy. 

The purpose of the fund is to scope, design, and manage coordinated research programs (CRPs), focused on making wild animal welfare interventions a reality. To do this, we’re prioritizing work that benefits both people and animals, often by working to solve some kind of wildlife conflict. While I believe we should work to solve all kinds of wild animal welfare issues, things that significantly benefit people and resolve conflicts will be more tractable to implement sooner. 

We’re currently hiring for program managers to scope and manage CRPs. If you’re looking for varied work and high autonomy, this might be for you. Please share widely!

I can’t thank Wild Animal Initiative enough for doing the foundational work that makes this Fund possible. WAI is where these ideas were borne and refined, and the team there is responsible for the fundamental insights that make identifying positive interventions possible. 

Over the next few months, I’ll share explanations of some of the program areas we’re exploring, and why they stand to help (at least) millions of people and billions of wild animals. For now, some Q&A. 

What is a coordinated research program?

CRPs are inspired by practices originally advanced at the US government agency DARPA (and described very thoroughly here). These programs are widely recognized as one of the best models for interdisciplinary, goal-oriented science. They are characterized by:

  • Top-down problem selection by expert program managers (PMs) who commit to fixed-term programs (typically 3–5 years).
  • Active management and milestone-driven accountability, rather than hands-off grant-giving.
  • Deliberate coordination among performers — building communities of researchers around novel problems and reducing the "weirdness barrier" that comes with working in a neglected area.
  • Easily-terminable contracts, which let PMs pivot funding away from approaches that aren't working and toward those that are.

Despite the popularity of the ARPA model in defense, biomedicine, energy, and climate, it has never previously been applied to animal welfare. The Wildlife Technology Fund exists to fill that gap.

Our CRPs will focus on two complementary pathways:

  • Translation — taking candidate interventions from initial theory to field-readiness. The science largely exists; no one has integrated the pieces into a deployable intervention.
  • Bottleneck removal — building the tools, metrics, and infrastructure that block many interventions at once. We cannot improve what we cannot measure, and we cannot target what we cannot monitor. Resolving an infrastructure bottleneck can unlock many downstream interventions.

How will the Fund work?

While details vary by focus area, most programs will follow a similar arc:

  • Scoping: A PM is assigned or proposes a direction, then runs a discovery process (research, interviews) and pitches a full program design — budget, translation plan, partners, and a clear case for why this topic warrants the CRP approach. It’s at this stage the program concepts get vetted to ensure they have a clear application planned for the end of their lifecycle, and that the math checks out on cost-effectiveness.
  • Development: Once approved, the PM identifies grantees through workshops, RFIs, and direct outreach. They also secure implementation partners: people or organizations that will carry forward the results of the program into the world. Small de-risking projects (e.g., tests of critical assumptions) can begin here.
  • Launch: The main body of work begins, often with multiple teams in parallel, coordinated tracks. The PM travels extensively, keeps teams on track, and builds community (e.g. a dedicated Slack workspace for cross-pollination).
  • Refinement:  Teams that aren't progressing or have hit intractable roadblocks are cut. The PM concentrates additional investment in the most promising directions. After this phase, we assess whether the program's original goals were met, and decide what (if anything) is needed to push prototypes into a deployable form.

A tech council of volunteer scientific and ethical experts advises the director on which programs to pursue. Crucially, only the director has final approval authority — this preserves coherent direction and avoids design-by-committee failure modes. 

What kinds of things will you focus on?

We have six CRP concepts ready to develop, and we aim to launch 2–3 of them in Year 1. (These will evolve as PMs do their discovery work; all are contingent on funding.)

  • Rodent fertility control. Develop agents that achieve high fertility reduction, substantial reductions in suffering versus rodenticides, comparable ecological effects, and high palatability. This program is being carried forward from Wild Animal Initiative’s existing work with Conservation X Labs on the topic.
  • Wild insect population monitoring. Build technology that can reliably estimate insect population sizes in the wild. Without this, we cannot evaluate the ecological or welfare consequences of almost any insect-relevant intervention.
  • Drone replacements for pollination services. Bring down the cost of micro-drones that can pollinate almond trees down to be cost-competitive with bee-based pollination services, potentially ending an industry that harms billions of bees each year.
  • Wildlife vaccination for high-suffering diseases. Identify diseases responsible for the largest welfare burdens and accelerate the development and deployment of vaccines that target them.
  • Bird-window collision ecological impacts. Complete the welfare and ecological analysis that bird-safe glass policy currently lacks, including off-target effects on insects and other prey species.
  • Welfare indicator discovery. Identify physiological or behavioral indicators that reliably correlate with affective state across many species and integrate over longer time scales, validated through standard processes.
  • Vulture conservation. Understanding the disease mitigation effects of larger vulture populations, for both people and animals, and determining if there are cost-effective ways to help conserve relevant species. 

Alongside the CRPs, we plan to work to train new program managers. ARPA-style grantmaking is a specialized skill, and the wild animal welfare community has almost no people trained in it. Talent development activities will give the Wildlife Technology Fund a pipeline of program ideas and talent, and will increase grantmaking capacity across the broader animal welfare ecosystem.

Why Renaissance Philanthropy?

Renaissance Philanthropy provides a great infrastructure and support for designing and running funds like this. I’ve received amazing support so far on strategy, program design, fundraising, and more. For more on the Renaissance Philanthropy model, see here. 

How can people support the Wildlife Technology Fund?

If you’re a scientist or otherwise a good fit to work on coordinating research programs in this area, or you’re interested in serving as an anchor donor for one of our programs, get in touch. If not, it helps a ton to just share our work (and the current job posting)!

item.title: We judge activism by the wrong measures: four ways we mismeasure whether protest works
item.description:
Published on October 5, 2026 4:07 PM GMT

Epistemic status: I've been an academic, climate activist and research lead in Extinction Rebellion UK's Data Analysis and Insights Circle. I co-authored most of the studies below. I am writing in a personal capacity, drawing on extensive research into climate activism.

Summary

  • People often decide whether a protest worked from a next-day poll or a hostile headline. I believe this is the wrong evidence.
  • I see four common mistakes: polling the public when the targets are elites, measuring too soon, trusting what people say over what they do, and generalising from one audience to another.
  • I end with five suggestions for funders and evaluators. Most apply to any movement that protests, including animal advocacy.

 

Most people in the UK accept that climate change is real, and most are worried about it. The majority (66%) even support nonviolent direct action to protect the UK's nature (Guardian). Yet very few take part in collective action. In 2023, five years after it was founded, only about 0.25% of the UK population (roughly 170,000 people) had joined Extinction Rebellion, a major climate activism group.

That gap between sympathy and participation is where a lot of arguments about whether protest "works" go wrong. Someone points to a poll showing the public dislikes a tactic, or a hostile headline the morning after, and concludes the action failed.

Since 2020, I have spent a lot of time studying climate activism. The work includes a review of 50 studies, national surveys, a field experiment with around 350,000 Facebook users, a media analysis and a survey of over 1,000 activists. My conclusion is that we often judge activism by the wrong measures. We poll the wrong audience, at the wrong time, using the wrong kind of data, and we generalise from the wrong people.

 

What the evidence can and can't tell us

With colleagues at Yale, I reviewed 50 recent, rigorous studies of collective climate action (open preprint). They covered protests, marches and divestment campaigns, drawn from sociology, psychology, political science and other fields. We sorted the findings by how strong the evidence was:

  • Strong: activism shifts public opinion and media coverage in a pro-climate direction, though effects vary by context and tactic.
  • Moderate: activism gets politicians talking about climate more, encourages pro-climate voting and puts financial pressure on carbon-intensive companies.
  • Suggestive: activism affects emissions and environmental policy.

The pattern is the problem. The evidence is strongest for outcomes close to the protest and weakest for the outcomes we care most about. That is not necessarily because activism fails at the distal end. Policy and emissions take years to move and have many causes, so they are hard to attribute. We also found little evidence that disruptive action reduced overall support for climate action, despite how often backlash is predicted. Social Change Lab's polling found the same for UK climate protests: disruptive actions didn't lead to a loss of public support for climate policies.

The review has two big gaps. Most studies come from the US and Western Europe, and most measure short-term outcomes. So when someone says "the evidence shows protest works" or "the evidence shows it backfires", usually the evidence shows effects on attention and opinion, measured soon after, in rich democracies.

 

Measure 1: polling the wrong audience

The most common test of a tactic is whether the public approves of it. With historian Kevin Young, I argued that majority support is the wrong metric. What matters more is whether a tactic imposes costs on the elite decision-makers who can concede.

Take the case of the 1963 Birmingham civil rights campaign. It did not win by persuading the white public. Boycotts and sit-ins cost downtown businesses millions in sales, and those businesses pressed politicians to accept desegregation. From this, we argued that disruption should impose direct costs on elites, it must be sustained so they cannot wait it out, and it can take many forms, including boycotts, litigation and financial pressure. For climate, that points towards the banks, insurers and investors that fund fossil fuels. This is an argument from history and theory rather than an empirical test, and one case is not proof.

The same applies to media coverage, the other thing activists check the morning after. With colleagues at Yale, Penn State and LSE, I analysed 412 articles about Extinction Rebellion and other groups. They came from the BBC and the 15 most-read UK papers, November 2022 to May 2023. We found:

  • Who writes the story matters a lot. On a scale from −1 (negative) to 1 (positive), conservative papers covered climate actions 0.25 points more negatively than neutral outlets and 0.52 points more negatively than liberal ones.
  • Tactics matter too. Legal actions were covered more favourably, and actions targeting industry got the most coverage. (Legal actions also got more coverage, but that difference was only significant in the full sample.)
  • Accuracy varied by outlet. In an exploratory analysis, conservative papers made more major factual errors.

The practical point: a hostile headline tells you a lot about the outlet and something about the tactic. On its own it is not a good guide to whether the tactic worked.

 

Measure 2: measuring at the wrong time

With colleagues at Social Change Lab, I co-authored a study that surveyed a nationally representative UK panel three times: before the protest (n = 1,986), days after (n = 1,657) and six months later (n = 1,356). We also surveyed a fresh representative sample at six months (n = 1,441) to compare the population as a whole against the baseline. There is also a longer report.

  • Days after: people who were aware of the protest held slightly more negative attitudes towards animals, and towards vegans. On its own, that looks like a backfire.
  • Six months later: awareness of the protest no longer predicted attitudes at all. The negative association had gone.
  • Mobilisation: on the day, donations to Animal Rising were 8.1 standard deviations above their daily mean, and sign-ups 5.3 standard deviations above.

In the fresh sample, attitudes towards animals were more positive at six months than before the protest. Without a comparison group we can’t credit that shift to the protest, but we can say that the short-term backlash did not last, while the boost to the group's own mobilisation was large.

This is just one protest, in one country, on one issue, but it shows how much the timing of a measurement can drive the verdict. A poll taken the next day would have reached the opposite conclusion to one taken six months later, and most commentary is written the next day.

 

Measure 3: trusting the wrong kind of data

Movements often design outreach around what people say they want. My research suggests that can mislead.

For Extinction Rebellion, I ran four focus groups with people who were sympathetic to climate action but not involved: grandparents, healthcare workers, religious people and scientists (summary). They were clear that they wanted to be asked politely and humbly. Even soft demands such as "do your bit" put them off, as did any hint of disruption.

We then tested this in a field experiment with around 354,000 Facebook users in Birmingham, Oxford and Cardiff. Ads invited people to a local climate talk. They used either a polite request or an urgent exhortation, with a protest, a diverse crowd or a flooded UK street as the image.

  • Exhortations beat requests, the opposite of what the focus groups said. They got a 0.54 percentage point higher click rate (overall clickthrough rate 1.7%.)
  • Flooding beat protest imagery by 0.22 percentage points.
  • The best combination, an exhortation with flood imagery, reached about 3.2% click-through in Birmingham. Effects varied by city and were weakest in Cardiff.

The outcome was clicks, not attendance, so this is one step along the path to action. But it is real behaviour, and it reversed what people told us.

A nationally representative survey of 1,100 UK adults found the same gap between saying and doing. At the end of the survey we asked people whether they would give up extra time, unpaid, to answer five more questions for XR. 32% did. Of those who had said they intended to donate money to climate action, fewer than half gave their time. A quarter of those who said they did not intend to donate gave it anyway.

The biggest difference was identity. 57% of people who identified with XR gave their time, 29 percentage points more than those who did not. That gap was about twice the size of the next largest: how much people prioritised climate, whether they thought XR was effective, and whether they intended to donate (each about 14 points).

 

Measure 4: generalising from the wrong people

The studies above point in different directions on disruption. The focus groups found that disruption put off newcomers. The Grand National protest brought a surge of new supporters. Both can be true, because they describe different people. I think disruption acts as a filter. It repels some people (e.g., those meeting a movement for the first time) but activates others (e.g., people who are already sympathetic).

Who is on the sympathetic side of that filter? In an online experiment with 5,996 UK adults that I ran for XR (unpublished), we showed people one of 11 climate narratives and asked how willing they were to join a large protest at Parliament. About 8% said they were very or extremely willing, and that group skewed strongly to the political left. Narratives about government corruption, the effectiveness of non-violent direct action and health impacts did best, and "green jobs" did worst. I don't think that makes green jobs a weak frame in general. My guess is that it appeals to the wrong audience: the people most moved by economic arguments are not the ones likely to turn up to a climate protest. 

The same split shows up among activists themselves. With colleagues, I surveyed 1,375 people on Extinction Rebellion UK's mailing list between December 2024 and January 2025. We asked how expecting repression (arrest, fines, surveillance) and having experienced it related to their intentions to take part in rule-following and rule-breaking action. 37.5% had experienced at least one form of repression.

  • Having experienced repression was correlated with stronger intentions to take disruptive action. Part of this ran through lower fear, consistent with the idea that people who have been through the system find it less frightening.
  • Expecting repression had no direct link to either type of action. It was linked to action indirectly, through emotion, in both directions: anger, outrage and contempt went with more action, while fear went with less disruptive action.
  • Belief that the movement could change government policy did not predict intentions. Beliefs about whether the movement can grow and whether one's own contribution matters may matter more.

The sample was older, whiter and better-off than the population, and many were retired, so the costs of repression may be heavier for others. Still, the pattern fits the filter idea. A response that deters the public at large may harden the committed core.

So a measure taken on one group tells you little about another. Public reaction to a disruptive action says little about its effect on existing supporters, and the reverse.

What this means for funders and evaluators

These are my suggestions, drawn from the studies above rather than tested directly.

  1. Measure effects on the people who can concede. Track pressure on targeted companies, financiers and decision-makers, not just public approval.
  2. Build in a later follow-up. A next-day poll and a six-month poll can disagree completely.
  3. Prefer behaviour to stated preference. Clicks, sign-ups, donations and turnout are imperfect, but they reversed what focus groups told us. A cheap field test often beats a survey of what people say they want.
  4. Separate audiences. Report effects on the general public, on sympathisers and on existing activists separately. An average hides the filter.
  5. Fund the gaps. The evidence base is thin outside rich democracies and on long-term policy and emissions outcomes. That is where marginal research money would go furthest.

None of this is specific to climate. I've focused on it because it's what I've studied, but most of these lessons apply to any movement that uses public protest.

References

My research (with co-authors):

  • Thomas-Walters, L., Scheuch, E. G., Ong, A. & Goldberg, M. H. (2025). The impacts of climate activism. Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences, 63. Preprint.
  • Young, K. A. & Thomas-Walters, L. What the climate movement's debate about disruption gets wrong. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications.
  • Scheuch, E. G., Ortiz, M., Shreedhar, G. & Thomas-Walters, L. (2024). The power of protest in the media: examining portrayals of climate activism in UK news. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 11, 270.
  • Ostarek, M., Klein, L., Rogers, C., Ozden, J., Thomas-Walters, L. (2025). Short and long-term effects of disruptive animal rights protest. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. Social Change Lab report.
  • Shreedhar, G., Hinton, J. & Thomas-Walters, L. (2026). Tell don't ask: how to use social media to mobilise local collective climate action. npj Climate Action.
  • Davies-Rommetveit, S., Douch, J., Gardner, P., Sach, A. A., Thomas-Walters, L. & Tausch, N. (2026). Emotional responses to state repression predict collective climate action intentions. Nature Climate Change, 16, 281–287.
  • Barriers to climate activism: the vital role of social identification. Preprint, SocArXiv.
  • Focus groups on recruitment messaging. One-page summary for Extinction Rebellion UK.

item.title: 40 hot takes
item.description:
Published on October 5, 2026 6:04 PM GMT

Note: This post was crossposted from the Coefficient Giving Farm Animal Welfare Research Newsletter by the Forum team, with the author's permission. The author may not see or respond to comments on this post.

Subtitle: On vegan advocacy, effective altruism, and FIFA

I turn 40 today. Here are some hot takes.

On factory farming

1. Our biggest challenge is salience. If factory farming led the evening news, it wouldn’t last long. This low salience is self-reinforcing: even people who care deeply about it seldom bring it up. Yuval Noah Harari thinks “the treatment of domesticated animals in industrial farms is perhaps the worst crime in history” — and almost never talks about it.

2. Our main opponent isn't the meat industry; it's inertia. If battery cages and gestation crates had always been illegal, the industry could never have gotten them legalized. Defending the status quo is just far easier than changing it.

3. The meat industry isn't the omnipotent Bond villain some activists imagine, forever scheming to win the grand battle over the future of meat. It's a bunch of middle managers in Tyson fleeces in a business park in Springdale, Arkansas, trying to hit their Q3 targets.

4. Factory farming is like tax havens, multi-level marketing schemes, and FIFA. Most people oppose it — but they care far less than the small minority who profit enormously from it.

5. None of us can truly internalize the vastness of the suffering factory farming causes. That’s a good thing. If we did, we’d go mad.

The future of farming

6. Every major technological revolution so far has hurt animals. The Agricultural Revolution confined them. The Scientific Revolution incubated animal testing. The Industrial Revolution put animals to work in mills and mines. Together, all three enabled factory farming. Will the AI Revolution be different?

7. Some assume cultivated meat will win once it's more efficient than farming animals. But when humanity was poor, it ate the most efficient foods: grains, roots, berries, scavenged meat. When it got richer, it could afford the luxury of inefficient foods it preferred — like meat. If it keeps getting richer, efficiency may matter even less.

8. Technology has no moral direction of its own. For the last century it mostly made animals' lives worse: denser cages, crueler genetics, and drugs to keep them alive in squalor. But it could just as easily make them better, through alternative proteins and humane farming tech. Which way it goes is partly up to us.

9. A post-factory-farming future will likely involve both alternative proteins and pasture-based meat. This prospect sometimes seems to distress the evangelists of each solution more than factory farming itself does.

10. We don’t lack the land to replace factory farming with pasture-based farms. We could pasture-raise every broiler chicken, egg-laying hen, and pig in America on an area about half the size of West Virginia. (Growing their feed would take another 35M acres — roughly the cropland we devote to corn for ethanol.)

11. The main problem with pasture-raised meat is that it costs more. But much of that premium is labor costs, which is to say jobs for farmers. If AGI brings both widespread wealth and mass unemployment, the price may stop mattering, and creating farm jobs may become popular enough to attract government subsidies.

Welfare reforms

12. We’ve already curtailed many bad practices, at least in the US and Europe: tethering sows, face branding cows, forced molting (starving) of hens, veal crates, docking cows’ tails, slaughtering mammals without effective stunning, and live-plucking birds. 13. Companies adopt animal welfare reforms when reform becomes the path of least resistance. Unsolicited dietary advice

16. Michael Pollan’s dietary advice is “Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.” My equally catchy version is “Eat plants. If you also eat animals, eat large ruminants like cows, not chickens or fish. 19. One reason “go vegan” became the dominant ask is that it matches the gravity of the situation. Saying “factory farming is evil, don’t buy from it on Mondays” just feels off. 22. Nature did not optimize for animal welfare. Darwin wrote that he couldn't believe a beneficent God had created the Ichneumonidae — parasitoid wasps whose larvae eat caterpillars alive from the inside, saving the vital organs for last to keep the meal fresh.

23. Intervening to help at least some wild animals shouldn’t be controversial. Wildlife rehabilitation centers take in injured animals regardless of whether a human or another wild animal hurt them. No one accuses them of playing God.

24. My favorite thing about EA is that it takes doing good as seriously as investors take making money. 26. My least favorite part of EA is something it also shares with top investors: hubris. EA was meant to be an endless search for the best ways to do good. Too many EAs act as if the search is over because they found the answer.

27. My favorite critique of EA begins "That isn't actually effective, because..." Once the argument is about what works — not what feels good, fits an ideology, or impresses donors — EA has already done its job.

Inside baseball

28. Our movement has an incredible set of driven, smart, relentless founders. They’ve built wildly effective groups. But many are poorly suited to running big organizations. They should hire a chief of staff or managing director so they can focus on what they’re best at — or step down and found something new.

29. Our movement also has an incredible set of strategic, creative, persistent campaigners. The best ones often get promoted into jobs where they spend more time in meetings than campaigning. They should get a raise instead, and be sent back to campaigning full-time.

30. Our movement needs stronger boards. That’s a great opportunity for talented supporters, especially those with board or executive experience, who can’t work in the movement full-time but want to get more involved.

31. If you're frustrated at how slowly society expands its moral circle, consider how slowly our own movement has expanded ours. It took us a century and a half to get from dogs and horses to farm animals, despite their vastly greater numbers. It took us a few more decades to get to chickens and fish, the most numerous farmed vertebrates. We've still barely reached shrimp and insects.

On strategy

32. Some advocates notice that successful social movements, like civil rights and suffrage, used tactics like marching and civil disobedience, and conclude those tactics must work for us too. They forget that plenty of failed movements — anarchism, temperance, pacifism — used the same tactics.

33. Factory farming is the rare issue where the populist right and the progressive left agree. That’s why I’m skeptical that bundling it with left-coded issues like climate change and environmental justice will broaden our coalition. For every progressive we pick up, we lose a conservative.

item.title: How much should we worry about the pneumonic plague lableak in Siberia?
item.description:
Published on October 5, 2026 5:42 PM GMT

Epistemic status: I wrote this up hoping people can poke holes in it because I am quite worried.

Here's what we've heard so far:

  • Local media is reporting that an employee of a BSL-3 lab in Irkutsk, Russia, died of pneumonic plague on Oct 1st.
  • The initial quarantine covered 200 people who were in contact with the employee before she died.
  • The FSB (Russian FBI) was seen assisting in the quarantine, which means it was not voluntary.
  • Soviet-era whistleblowers like Ken Alibek claim Irkutsk was a major bioweapon development facility. 
     

As of Oct 4th:

  • The quarantine has expanded to 5 hospitals in the area.
  • The Russian government has switched to denial/coverup. Local news sources have deleted mentions of "pneumonic plague." 

  • Local universities and schools have canceled some classes and extended mask mandates.
  • On the lab's website, they mention gain-of-function research for making bacteria more virulent.  
  • The White House is monitoring the suspected outbreak.

Why this might be a big deal

  • Regular pneumonic plague is maybe not that hard to deal with (?) but if it is a bioweapon that was leaked, it could be significantly more virulent than, say, COVID. Pneumonic plague has an R0 of ~1.3-3.5, whereas genetically engineered variants could have an R0 of 5-12.   
  • If there is only one infection, then why quarantine 5 hospitals?
  • If it wasn't a big deal, the Russian government wouldn't put much effort into covering it up. This is something I'll monitor over the coming few days.
  • If this is a bioweapon, this could be quite bad. In Annie Jacobson's latest book, Biological War: A Scenario, much of the world is dead within the first few weeks after the first infection. I found it to be realistic, and it is a big reason I'm so worried. The scenario started basically identically to what's happening here.
  • I asked the AIs if pneumonic plague is treatable with antibiotics, and they quoted me that the death rate with treatment is still between 8-30%.
  • Soviet whistleblowers say they have successfully created recombinant plague with antibacterial resistance and much higher virulence, so we know it's possibly a bioweapon.

 

Why this might not be a big deal

  • Some OSINT researchers looked at a bunch of street cams in Irkutsk and didn't find anything really out of the ordinary. Life is continuing basically as normal there.
  • Nothing ever happens.
  • We don't really have much info on the whole thing. There are no reported second cases from officials, but with historical evidence, we should assume a cover-up- e.g., the Sverdlovsk anthrax leak in 1979 and COVID-19 in China. So evidence that there are no secondary cases is not really (much) evidence.
  • If it's not a bioweapon, it's most likely fine.
  • Some smart bio people I know think this is not a big deal, but I don't really understand their reasons why.
  • Superforecasters at Sentinel think that the odds of pandemic are <1%. Their reasoning is that there is no official reporting of any further cases, and that the Russian government is implementing strict quarantine measures.
    • But I think this is actually the opposite of good news. The fact that the Russian FSB is implementing a strict quarantine AND the fact that the government is in full information control mode, denying that it is even pneumonic plague anymore, pushes me in the direction of this being a big deal, and they are covering it up.
      • I would be persuaded this isn't a big deal if the Russian government wasn't covering it up AND was implementing a strict quarantine, but because they are doing both, it makes me think it is, in fact, a big deal.

10/5 update:

  • Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan are now doing screening health checks at the Russian border to contain the spread of pneumonic plague.
  • Russian equivalent of HHS is now denying there was any accident at the lab at all.
  • Unconfirmed: reports of antibiotics running out in the city of Irkutsk
  • Kevin Esvelt is saying that it's either a bioweapon or it's not plague.
    • Another thread by Esvelt here.

 

10/6 update:

  • According to an OSINT researcher, the patient zero who died, Daria Shipilova, coauthored a paper that tested antibiotic resistance from plague.
  • I updated a lot on Esvelt thinking this was likely a bioweapon, but because not much news came out today, I think it's much less likely to become an epidemic.

Please let me know anything else I'm missing here.
